1.pericope_label: Jerubbaal pitched beside the well of Harod

schools.summary: Gill notes only that Jerubbaal was the name his father had lately given him.

Henry attends to the hour and the ground. He rose early, as one whose heart was upon his business and afraid of losing time; now that he is sure God is with him he is impatient of delay, and faith in God's promises must not slacken but rather quicken our endeavours. He pitched near a famous well so his army might not want water, and gained the higher ground, the enemy lying beneath him in the valley. On the reduction that follows Henry reads the whole as a provision that the praise be reserved to God. Thirty-two thousand was a small force beside what Midian had brought into the field, and their leader was ready to think them too few when God told him they were too many. He gives three reasons. God would show that when he employs suitable instruments he does not need them, being not indebted to them for their service, but they to him for their employment. He would shame those who had tamely submitted to Midian for the disproportion of numbers, since they now saw that had they made sure of God's favour, one of them might have chased a thousand. And he would exclude boasting, which is the reason given in the text itself — for my own hand hath saved me is a word that must never come out of the mouth of such as shall be saved, and he that glories must glory in the Lord. The first winnowing dismissed the fearful, and Henry pauses on the law providing for such a proclamation, which their leader may have thought applied only to wars for enlarging their coast, not to a necessary defence, so he would not have proclaimed it unbidden. Cowards would be as likely as any to take the honour from God after a victory, and so God would not do them the honour of employing them. One would have thought scarcely an Israelite would own himself fearful under such a leader, yet more than two parts in three filed off. Some think the long oppression had broken their spirits; Henry thinks it likelier that consciousness of their own guilt had taken away their courage, since sin stared them in the face and therefore they durst not look death in the face. Faint-hearted people are not fit to be employed for God, and among those enlisted under Christ's banner there are more such than we think.

Clarke says the second name had become a surname from the incident of the altar, and reaches the root of Harod, which signifies to shake through fear, but refers it forward to the panic that seized the Midianite host at this place.

Ellicott sets the double name among the Scriptural characters who carry two, and presses the topography through the preposition: the word rendered beside is rather above, since it would have been dangerous to encamp on the plain. The name of the spring means trembling, which he takes for an allusion to the timidity of the people the next verses describe, so that it is used here by anticipation. He adds that the name occurs here only, and that since the camp lay on Gilboa it must be the abundant spring at the foot of the hill now called the spring of Goliath, from a mistaken legend that the giant died there. Of the hill he is more cautious. The only Moreh known from elsewhere is at Shechem, five and twenty miles south, so the word must here stand for Little Hermon, the Latin turning it into a lofty hill, perhaps to avoid a supposed difficulty. Since Moreh means archer, Ellicott suggests Little Hermon may have been the Archer's Hill, from the bowmen of the Amalekites.

debates.question: Why is the spring called Harod, 'trembling'?

positions.position: from the timidity of the Israelites described in the next verses — the name used by anticipation
from the terror and panic that seized the Midianite host at this place

outliers.note: traces the cowardice not to the long oppression but to guilt: sin stared them in the face, and therefore they durst not look death in the face

themes: the camp at the well of Harod

2.pericope_label: By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you

schools.summary: Gill observes the odds were heavy before any reduction at all, thinks Gideon would not have made the proclamation unbidden, and may have taken the law to concern wars of conquest only. On the water test he lays both readings side by side without deciding, noting that Ben Gersom took the kneelers for slothful and the lappers for courageous, which agrees with the earlier dismissal. He concludes that with food in one hand and a trumpet in the other the three hundred were unarmed, so the salvation would most clearly appear to be the Lord's.

Clarke gives the reason from the other end: had a numerous host been led up, the excellence of the power that discomfited the enemy might have seemed of man and not of God, whereas the manner of the whole made both nations see that the thing was of God — inspiring the one with confidence and the other with fear. On the crux of mount Gilead he reports the suggestion of two Gileads, and the conjecture that the text should read Gilboa, which no manuscript countenances; he prefers the solution that many eastern Manassites from Gilead were in the army, more afraid of their Midianite neighbours than the western tribes, so the sense is, whosoever from Gilead is fearful, let him go home. Twenty-two thousand went, and Clarke is astonished that so many would fight neither for God nor for their country — though he allows that slavery debases the mind, and that if the armies of Europe had the same address from their generals, an equal proportion would go home. On the lapping he adds that the verb reproduces the very sound a dog makes in drinking.

Keil sets the arithmetic out: the Israelite force stood at thirty-two thousand and Midian with its allies at about a hundred and thirty-five thousand, so the disproportion was already great when the Lord called the smaller number too many, the Hebrew being comparative. He is firm that the three hundred were not the cowardly or indolent, and explains the action as taking water in the hollow of the hand and lapping it in. Ellicott says the reduction must have put Gideon's faith to a severe trial. The proclamation that follows is exactly the law's, and he notes what that law rests on: cowardice is contagious, so timid men are a direct danger. He cites the rule kept by Judas Maccabaeus and by Epaminondas before Leuctra, with the Roman remark that even where there are many legions it is always the few that win. The word rendered depart early occurs only here: the Chaldee explains it as in the morning, another renders it hastily, like a bird, and Keil connects it with an Arabic root meaning to twist round, hence to slink away by by-paths — Ellicott hears contempt in it. On mount Gilead he adds that Gilead was a son of Abiezer, so the name may have been a rallying-cry of Manasseh, the phrase meaning let him leave that camp. On the water test he reports Josephus, who has the men brought down in the noon heat and judges those who flung themselves down the braver and the hasty lappers the cowards, Theodoret making the divine aid appear in the choosing of the most timid; but Ellicott thinks greater self-control is shown by stooping and drinking from the hand than by falling at full length. He passes on the rabbinic notion that those who knelt were secret idolaters who had bowed to Baal. On the provisions he prefers the ancient versions, which make the three hundred take the victuals and trumpets of the rest: supplies would be scarce near so vast a host, and but for this verse we might wonder how each got a horn.

debates.question: Were the three hundred lappers the bravest men or the most timid?

positions.position: the bravest — greater self-control is shown by stooping and drinking from the hand than by falling at full length
certainly not the cowardly or indolent
undecidable from the text; Ben Gersom took the kneelers for slothful, Josephus held the reverse

debates.question: What does 'from mount Gilead' mean, when the camp lay near Gilboa?

positions.position: eastern Manassites from Gilead were in the army — whosoever from Gilead is fearful, let him go home
Gilead may have been a rallying-cry of Manasseh generally, so the sense is, let him leave that camp

outliers.note: grounds the law of dismissing the fearful on the observation that cowardice is contagious, citing Judas Maccabaeus and Epaminondas before Leuctra

themes: the people are yet too many

9.pericope_label: A cake of barley bread tumbled into the host of Midian

schools.summary: Gill observes that though it was the dead of night, something would be heard — a clear proof, he thinks, of God's foreknowledge. He dwells on the word for the interpretation, which means a breaking: the dream was like something sealed, its reading like a nut whose kernel cannot be got at till the shell is broken.

Henry sees the point at once: the army being cut to a handful, its captain must fight by faith or not at all, and so God provides recruits for his faith instead of his forces. He is given a word of command to warrant an action that otherwise looked rash, and a word of promise to assure him of a success that looked improbable; and it came the same night, when he may be supposed full of care — divine consolations are given to believers not only strongly but seasonably. Then he is made his own spy. God knows the infirmities of his people, Henry says, and what great encouragement they may take from a small matter, and so, knowing what would be said in that quarter of the camp, he sends him to hear it. Phurah goes as one he could confide in and a witness besides, that the word might be established out of the mouth of two — two being better than one, and a little help better than none. Henry notes the sight that met them: men like grasshoppers for multitude, though they proved no better than grasshoppers for courage. He is blunter about the dream, calling it foolish, as our dreams generally are, since in the multitude of them there are many vanities; the interpretation he calls far-fetched. Yet he grants how apt the resemblance turns out — a man who had threshed corn and made cakes fitly figured by a cake, his force as inconsiderable as a cake of a little flour, and as unlikely to overthrow that army as a cake to overturn a tent. But after all, he asks, do not interpretations belong to God?

Clarke reads the promise as a thing already done — I have determined it, and it is as sure as if accomplished. He supposes the multitude, having come merely for plunder, was unarmed but kept guards on the outside as caravans do, and it was to these the two came; and he says flatly that both dream and interpretation were inspired, to increase one man's confidence and appal his enemies.

Keil says of the Hebrew tense that it denotes a purpose already formed, and takes the term for the outposts as the foremost of the fighting men. Ellicott measures the nerve this took against a more famous three hundred: the courage went beyond Thermopylae, since these were to attack in the open plain, not hold a pass. What Gideon was to hear he identifies as the omen the Jews called the daughter of a voice — sometimes a voice from heaven, sometimes an echo, sometimes the first chance words a man hears after being bidden to watch for them. It ranked as one of four modes of divine direction, with prophets, dreams and Urim, though lowest of the four. He renders the word for the outposts literally as ranks by five and thinks it means sentries. On the cake he reports that the noun occurs nowhere else and the rabbinic derivations yield no sense, while the Chaldee, the Greek, the Latin and Josephus all make it a cake baked on coals, as the desert Arabs still bake dough in ashes. That it was barley he thinks the point of the symbol, Josephus adding that men can hardly eat such bread. The raids had reduced Israel to living on it, and if the Midianites were used to taunting Gideon's people as eaters of barley bread, as later Bedouins do, the application would be the more natural — Josephus has the soldier say that as barley is the vilest seed, so Israel was the vilest people of Asia.

debates.question: Why is the cake in the dream barley?

positions.position: because barley bread was proverbially the coarsest food, and Israel had been reduced to it — perhaps a standing Midianite taunt
because a cake fitly figured a man who had threshed corn and baked, and a force as inconsiderable as a little flour

outliers.note: classes the overheard words as the Bath Kol, the lowest of the four recognised modes of divine direction

themes: the barley cake and its meaning

16.pericope_label: He divided the three hundred into three companies, with trumpets and pitchers

schools.summary: Gill gives the practical reason for three companies of a hundred: partly to make a show of an army with right and left wing, partly to fall on the camp at different points.

Henry sets the attack beside Abraham's rescue of Lot: the numbers nearly the same, both leaders divided their forces, both struck by night, both conquered under great disadvantage — Gideon a son of Abraham by descent, as the Midianites also were through Keturah, but an heir of his faith besides. He sees in the outfit a design to make the rout not only fatal but shameful. A trumpet in the right hand and a pitcher with a torch in the left is to jest at an enemy, going out as against children rather than soldiers, so that the daughter of Zion laughs them to scorn. In the order to watch him Henry hears the word of command the captain of our salvation gives his soldiers, having left us an example with a charge to follow it. He adds that in the night all frights are most frightful, and that fewness favoured secrecy, so small a party reaching the camp unnoticed. He sets out three instruments of terror: a great noise, each man blowing his horn and dashing his pitcher, probably against his neighbour's so that both broke together — itself a figure of what followed when the Midianites killed one another; a great blaze, the torches hid like a candle under a bushel and then flashing through the camp like lightning, perhaps firing the outer tents; and a great shout. On the cry Henry would read it for the Lord and for Gideon, the word sword not standing in the Hebrew here, and thinks it borrowed from the dream, the name that had proved a terror being turned against them but with the divine name prefixed, without which his own was an insignificant cypher.

Clarke draws a lesson from the arrangements: though the victory was to be from the Lord, prudential means were still used — had they not been, it is not likely God would have delivered the enemy up, for even in working a miracle he will have natural means employed, as when a man was told to dip in Jordan or wash in Siloam. On the war-cry he holds the word sword genuine, absent here but present in the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic and in eight collated manuscripts.

Ellicott notes that dividing an attacking force was a common stratagem, used by Saul against Ammon and by David against Absalom; and he sees the point of the horns, since hearing three hundred the Midianites would suppose three hundred companies were upon them. He identifies the vessels as earthenware jars, the word being cognate with our cask, so the Latin rendering by flagons is mistaken; the lamps he takes for firebrands or torches rather than lamps proper. His best illustration is a modern one: the police officer of Cairo carried at night a torch which burns without flame once lit, blazing up when waved, and answering the purpose of a dark lantern, its burning end concealed in a small pot when light was not wanted. On the order to watch him, Ellicott says he showed all three hundred what he wished done at the signal, which his own hundred would give. Keil places the beginning of the middle watch at midnight, and Ellicott explains that the Jews divided the night into three watches, the four-watch reckoning being later borrowed from the Romans, so the attack fell soon after ten, when the host would be in its first sleep; the words about the watch being newly set mean the assault came while the guard was changing. On the cry he thinks the word sword better omitted, the phrase being literally for Jehovah and for Gideon, like the watchword Cyrus gave his soldiers.

debates.question: Does the word 'sword' belong in the war-cry at verse 18?

positions.position: yes; it is absent here but stands in the Chaldee, Syriac and Arabic and in eight collated manuscripts
better omitted — the phrase is literally for Jehovah and for Gideon
read it for the Lord and for Gideon, the word not standing in the Hebrew here

outliers.note: insists that prudential means were indispensable even to a victory wholly from the Lord, since God will have natural means used even in working a miracle

themes: the sword of the LORD and of Gideon

20.pericope_label: They stood every man in his place, and the LORD set every man's sword against his fellow

schools.summary: Gill says they stood to see the salvation of God, and that had they gone in they could have done nothing, having no weapons; but their standing increased the terror, since the enemy might suppose they stood either to light a large army in behind them or to light the forces already among them while these destroyed them — the latter seeming what possessed them, since they fell to killing their fellows. They kept blowing to increase the fright, and stood as torch-bearers to light the Midianites in destroying one another.

Clarke asks the reader to picture it: in a dark night, the sudden glare of three hundred torches on the half-awakened eyes of the enemy, with the clangour of three hundred trumpets mingled with the thundering shout. He reads the standing still the same way as Gill: each company kept its station and sounded on, and the enemy, believing these the trumpets of a numerous army already within the camp, turned their swords against every man they met while trying to escape. No stratagem, he says, was ever better imagined, better executed, or more completely successful. He also collects the allegories the passage has attracted. Origen made the three hundred types of the preachers of the gospel, their trumpets the preaching of Christ crucified, their torches the conduct of righteous men; and some verses against Marcion turn them into horsemen and find in the number the mystery of the cross, since the Greek letter standing for three hundred is itself the shape of a cross. Clarke prints the verses, then gives his verdict: we see here what abstruse meanings a strong imagination, assisted by a little piety, may extract from what was never intended as a mystery.

Keil supplies the detail that gave the illusion its force: the three hundred stood without moving, so the enemy necessarily supposed a numerous army was advancing behind the torch-bearers. He renders the outcry as anguish, and the next verb as carrying off — the enemy hurrying away tents and herds. Ellicott observes that the men were by that arrangement comparatively defenceless, a horn in one hand and a brand in the other, though a shield might hang on the left arm and a sword be girded on the thigh. Startled from sleep in a camp imperfectly protected, the Midianites would see blazing lights on every side and hear horns and a war-cry from every quarter; and the first thought to rise would be that treachery was at work among the motley elements of the camp itself. The result was a wild panic like that which seized the Persians at Plataea — and even a well-disciplined camp, Ellicott adds, is liable to such outbursts, as the Ten Thousand were, whose commander next morning proclaimed a reward for whoever would say who had let the ass loose, a joke afterwards used to shame soldiers out of groundless alarms. He collects the parallels. One ancient writer on the art of war records a commander attacking Heraea who set his trumpeters apart to sound a charge from many quarters, so that the townsmen, thinking the region crowded with enemies, abandoned it. Hannibal once escaped Fabius Maximus by tying torches to the heads of cattle, and an Arab chief of the eighteenth century used trumpets in exactly this manner, with the same success. Ellicott takes the running and crying as men casting about to learn what the blast meant, their cries the wail of despair or confused words of command; and he sets the mutual slaughter beside the Ammonites and Moabites destroying each other before Jehoshaphat. Of the places named he can say little: the house of the acacia, from trees still abundant there; the meadow of the dance, native place of Elisha; and a name meaning famous, whose site is unknown. Clarke observes that most occur nowhere else in Scripture.

debates.question: Why did the three hundred not charge into the camp?

positions.position: they had no weapons, and their standing still increased the terror — the enemy took them for torch-bearers lighting a slaughter already begun
standing motionless made the enemy suppose a numerous army was advancing behind the torch-bearers

outliers.note: prints Origen's allegory and the anti-Marcionite verses that find the cross in the number three hundred, then dismisses the whole as imagination assisted by a little piety

themes: they stood every man in his place

23.pericope_label: They took two princes of the Midianites, Oreb and Zeeb

schools.summary: Gill notes that the men who gathered were not out of all the tribes but those lying nearest, and that the point of summoning Ephraim was to get the fords first. On the names he gives them as raven and wolf, and thinks them either nicknames fastened on them for cruelty or titles taken to make themselves feared.

Henry is sharper about the returning men. Those afraid to fight now took heart when the worst was over, and were ready enough to divide the spoil though backward to make the onset; yet he distinguishes them from the hired troops of a later reign who went home in a rage, for these waited for an opportunity of service, though denied the honour of forcing the lines. He sees the trap closing: they took the waters, posting themselves along the river side, so that those fleeing from their pursuers fell into the hands of the men waiting to intercept them — here were fear, and the pit, and the snare. Now that the enemy had begun to fall, he adds, it was easy to say, Down with them. On the two princes Henry gives the point an edge: the places of their shelter were made the places of their slaughter, and the man who destroyed them had himself, for fear of them, lately hidden his corn by a winepress. He closes with a wish: that where help is needed it were as willingly given as here, and that when a good work is begun we were as ready to welcome fellow-labourers as we often are to hinder one another.

Clarke takes the pursuers for men sent home the day before, who on hearing of the rout went straight after the enemy. He takes Beth-barah for the place where Israel forded Jordan under Joshua, and thinks the Midianites made for it and were there overthrown. Of the two princes he has one taking shelter in the cavern of a rock and the other in the vat of a winepress, both afterwards called by their names; and he enlarges the point about their names, since in all ancient nations generals took names from birds and beasts, the Romans having their jackdaws, crows and eagles, and we ourselves our Crows, Wolfs, Lyons and Hawkes. Of the heads carried to Gideon he observes that among barbarous nations the head of a conquered chief was commonly brought to the conqueror, as Pompey's to Caesar, and that for the credit of human nature it is a pity such things were ever done.

Keil says plainly that those of Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh had been dismissed before the battle and were on their way back, and could be recalled quickly; the omission of Zebulun he puts down to brevity. Since the waters are named before the Jordan and distinguished from it, he takes them for the brooks the flying men would have to cross before reaching the river, and reports that even Eusebius could give nothing definite about Beth-barah. Ellicott adds that Naphtali and Asher would chase the fugitives northward and Manasseh those who made for the lower fords, and notices the timing of the summons to Ephraim: their leader had not ventured to call on these haughty clansmen until the victory was assured. He glosses the phrase as intercepting the flight, and takes the waters for marshes formed by streams running from the Ephraim hills down to the Jordan; the name Beth-barah he renders house of the waste, against Jerome's house of the well. On the princes he is more cautious than the rest, holding such names common among nomads and no mark of scorn. He renders the first site as the raven's rock, mentioned again only once, in a prophet recalling the slaughter of Midian there; and he points out that the closing notice is given by anticipation, the crossing of the Jordan not being related till the next chapter, and that the rout left its mark on the national memory, the prophets needing only to speak of the day of Midian.

debates.question: Are Oreb and Zeeb, raven and wolf, names given in scorn?

positions.position: either nicknames fastened on them for cruelty or titles taken to make themselves feared
no; such names are common among nomads, and in all ancient nations generals took names from birds and beasts

outliers.note: notices that Ephraim was not summoned until the victory was assured, their leader not venturing to call on those haughty clansmen sooner

themes: the dismissed men return for the pursuit
